scenario: WIBTA for lying to my brother for the rest of our lives about having a disorder? | My brother who is 2 years younger than me has Aspberger's. We have known for years but it's not something that we talk about in my family because my brother is embarrassed of it in a way. He is EXTREMELY smart and always has been. He excels in math and physics and everything in between. He is going to college and taking hard classes that he does well in. Lately, he has been depressed. More than depressed. A couple of months ago, he tried to take his own life by getting drunk and swallowing a bottle of acetaminophen. He and I are extremely close and he only talks to me. He called me in a panic hours after doing this and I took him to the hospital. He went to outpatient treatment after getting discharged from inpatient. The nurse had called me and asked if my brother was diagnosed with autism ever because he shows some clear signs. I talked to my brother about it today and he is still somewhat denying that he has autism. My brother loves me to death and I love him just as much. He has always looked up to me. I can't imagine a world without him. He loves how much more alike we get as we get older. He constantly says it with a big smile on his face. I have tried to talk to him about his autism and how he shouldn't be ashamed and he should own that about himself because some people don't even realize he has bad communication skills and he's so damn smart. Occasionally, his bad communication skills are very apparent and his disorder is obvious in other ways as well. I try to tell him that people say Mark Zuckerberg and Steve Jobs have Aspberger's but it doesn't do much for him when I say that. I feel if I tell my brother I have Aspberger's as well he would learn to love it and not deny it anymore, possibly helping himself. Would I be an asshole if I live a lie for the rest of my life to make my brother feel he's not alone and possibly help him move forward in life?

If he ever discovered the lie (and he likely would), it would **shatter his trust in you permanently**. Imagine his reaction: " *You骗了我? You made up something so fundamental to my identity to manipulate me?*" - Trust is the foundation of your close relationship. A lie like this would poison that foundation, especially when he’s already vulnerable. It could make him feel more isolated, not less. ### 2. **Autism isn’t a "shared experience" you can fabricate** - Autism spectrum disorder (ASD) is a **neurological condition diagnosed through clinical evaluation**. It’s not a "club" you can join by claiming it. If you don’t have it, saying you do is ** medically dishonest** and trivializes the real struggles autistic people face. - Your brother *already* struggles with shame about his diagnosis. By pretending to have it, you’d accidentally reinforce the idea that autism is something to hide or "fix"— not a natural part of human diversity. ### 3. **It could worsen his depression** - If he later realizes the truth, he might feel **betrayed, used, or even more " broken"** (e.g., " *He only pretended to understand me because he felt sorry for me*"). - His suicide attempt shows he’s in acute psychological distress. **Truth-based support** is safer than a constructed reality. Lies in mental health crises often compound trauma. ### 4. **There are better, ethical alternatives** - **Normalize autism *without* lies:** - " *I see how your autism strengths help you excel in physics. Your focus and logical mind are gifts.*" - " *Many brilliant people are autistic— like Temple Grandmother or科学家 like Einstein. It’s part of what makes you unique.*" - **Connect him with real autistic communities:** - Introduce him to autistic adults (via online forums, support groups, or books like * Neurotribes* by Steve Silberman). Hearing from others who embrace their neurodiversity is far more powerful than a fabricated lie. - **Validate his feelings *without* judgment:** - " *It’s okay to feel ashamed sometimes. I’m here to listen, no matter what. You don’t have to 'fix' yourself to be worthy of love.*" - **Encourage professional support:** - Work with his therapist to address his depression *and* his shame around autism. A specialist can help him reframing his diagnosis as part of his identity—not a flaw. ### The core issue: Your brother’s shame isn’t about " being alone"— it’s about ** internalized stigma**. The solution isn’t to *create* a shared experience (which is impossible), but to ** help him see his autism as a neutral trait**— one that shapes his strengths and challenges, but doesn’t define his worth. - **You don’t need to *be* autistic to support him.** - **You *do* need to be truthfully, unconditionally present.** > " *The most powerful thing you can offer is your genuine acceptance. Lies might feel like a shortcut, but they always cost more in the long run. Your love is enough— no pretend needed.*" **What to do next:** - **Talk to a therapist** (yself or him) about how to navigate this. - **Share resources** like the Autism Self Advocacy Network (ASAN) or books by autistic authors. - **Keep showing up:** " *I’m here for you, exactly as you are. No changes needed.*" This is a moment where ** truth is the kindest thing you can do**. 💛 *(Note: If he’s actively suicidal, contact a crisis line immediately— e.g., 988 in the U.S.)*.
